Kill
kĭl
v. (to deprive of life; in the sixth commandment, the KJV's rendering of a Hebrew verb that means specifically to murder)
From Middle English killen, to strike or beat — probably a variant of quell, Anglo-Saxon cwellan, to kill. The English word covers every kind of life-taking, which is exactly the difficulty in the sixth commandment.

Biblical Definition

“Thou shalt not kill” (Exo 20:13) is four words in English and two in Hebrew, and the Hebrew is more precise than the English. The verb is ratsach, which Scripture uses for murder and for manslaughter — unlawful private killing — and never for the execution of a criminal by the magistrate, for the taking of life in a lawful war, or for the slaughter of animals. Different Hebrew verbs cover those. The commandment therefore forbids the man to take life on his own authority; it does not disarm the magistrate whom God has appointed to bear the sword (Rom 13:4), and it does not contradict the same law-code that prescribes capital penalties a few chapters later. The Lord Jesus extends the commandment inward to anger and contempt (Mat 5:21-22) without loosening it outward. He also sets the fear of man in its place: “fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell” (Mat 10:28). And He names the thief who comes “to steal, and to kill, and to destroy” against Himself, who came that they might have life (Joh 10:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines kill as to deprive of life, by any means; to put to death; to slay — noting that it is applied to men, to animals, and figuratively to plants.

expand to see more

KILL, v.t. To deprive of life, animal or vegetable, in any manner or by any means.

2. To butcher; to slaughter for food.

3. To quell; to appease; to calm; to still; as, to kill the pain.

Note. The Hebrew word in the sixth commandment signifies properly to murder, and is not used of the execution of justice or of lawful war.

Note. Fear not them which kill the body. Matt. x.

Key Scripture

Exo 20:13 — "Thou shalt not kill."

Mat 10:28 — "And fear not them which kill the body, but are not able to kill the soul: but rather fear him which is able to destroy both soul and body in hell."

Joh 10:10 — "The thief cometh not, but for to steal, and to kill, and to destroy: I am come that they might have life, and that they might have it more abundantly."

Ecc 3:3 — "A time to kill, and a time to heal; a time to break down, and a time to build up;"

Modern Corruption

“Thou shalt not kill” is quoted flatly against capital punishment and lawful defence, while the same six words are treated as inapplicable to the unborn.

expand to see more

The pacifist and abolitionist use of Exo 20:13 rests entirely on the breadth of an English verb. The Hebrew ratsach is the language of unlawful private killing; the Torah that gives the commandment also commands the death penalty for murder in the very next chapter, and grounds it in Gen 9:6 on the image of God in the victim. Rom 13:4 says the magistrate bears the sword as the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath. To read the sixth commandment as forbidding what the same law requires is to make Scripture contradict itself within a page.

The far graver corruption runs the other way. The commandment's actual target — the taking of innocent human life by private hands — describes abortion exactly, and the argument that the unborn child is not yet a neighbour collapses against the Bible's own account of that child: knit together in the womb (Psa 139:13-16), known and sanctified before birth (Jer 1:5), leaping in his mother's womb at the greeting of Mary (Luk 1:41). Exo 21:22-25 assigns penalties for harm done to a woman with child. A culture that reads the sixth commandment as forbidding the execution of a convicted murderer and permitting the destruction of an unborn child has inverted it at both ends.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Middle English killen, to strike; rendering Hebrew ratsach (H7523), to murder or slay unlawfully, distinct from harag, to slay, and shachat, to slaughter for sacrifice; Greek apokteino (G615), to kill.

expand to see more

Hebrew ratsach (H7523) — to murder; the verb of the sixth commandment, used of murder and manslaughter, never of judicial execution or lawful war.

Hebrew harag (H2026) — to slay, kill; the general verb, used of killing in battle and of judicial death.

Hebrew shachat (H7819) — to slaughter, as a sacrificial victim; the altar's verb.

Hebrew muth (H4191) in the causative — to put to death; the verb of the death penalty in the statutes.

Greek apokteino (G615) — to kill, put to death; Mat 10:28, where the body may be killed and the soul cannot.

Usage

"“Thou shalt not kill” — Hebrew ratsach, unlawful private killing."

"“Kill the body… not able to kill the soul” — the limit of what any persecutor can reach."

"“A time to kill, and a time to heal” — the Preacher's catalogue of appointed seasons."
